The first thing that comes is the number itself: one thousand. It sits at the edge of the page like a fence. I keep thinking about how a word limit is both a room and a door. It closes the party politely and says, now, after all this talking, what did you actually mean? So I begin with a small inventory of what arrives uninvited: the smell of rain on warm pavement, a blue chair in an empty apartment, the sound a coin makes when it falls into a vending machine and does not buy anything. These are not important things, but importance is a suspect category. Most of my life has been assembled from unremarkable moments that later turned out to be load-bearing.

There is a window across the room. Through it I can see a man walking a dog that is walking him. The sky is a color that has no good name—not gray, not white, not blue, but the color of a television turned off in a house where someone is still awake. I think about how every city is a collection of private weathers. Two people can stand on the same corner, one remembering a funeral, the other wondering whether to buy oranges. The street does not arbitrate. It only continues.

I once read that the word “consider” comes from the Latin for “to look at the stars.” I don’t know if that’s true, but I like the idea that thinking is a way of consulting the sky. Maybe that is what I am doing now: considering. Looking up without lifting my head. The stars are not visible, but they are there, which is the basic condition of most of what we love. The dead are there. The absent are there. The future is there, wearing its coat, waiting to be introduced. We are always talking to things we cannot see, and sometimes the conversation is all we have.

When I was a child, I believed that if I held my breath while a car passed, I had to make a wish. If I forgot, something small would go wrong: a pencil would break, a sock would go missing, a teacher would call on me for the one question I hadn’t read. This is how superstition works—it gives your anxiety a job. You hand fear a little broom and tell it to sweep the porch. It sweeps and sweeps, and while it is sweeping, you live. Maybe that is also what writing is. You give the formless thing a task. Put the chairs in a row. Describe the rain. Keep the sentence moving until the sentence becomes a path, and by walking it you discover where you were going.

I wonder sometimes what it would be like to be a word. Not a grand word like “justice” or “threshold,” but a small, useful one: “spoon,” “unless,” “slightly.” To be “slightly”: to live always at the margin of comparison. To be “unless”: to carry a door inside your meaning and hold it open for exception. Words are strange creatures. They have ancestors. They migrated. They changed their clothes. They were stolen, borrowed, misspelled, sung. “Good-bye” was once “God be with ye,” a blessing worn down by hurry. “Nice” used to mean foolish. “Awful” used to mean full of awe. We are speaking with the fossils of old feelings and calling it conversation.

I like the idea that every person is a library with the lights on but the doors locked. We pass each other and see the glow under the door. Occasionally someone knocks. Occasionally we open. But there is never enough time to read the whole collection. This is why love is partly a decision to stop reading and start believing. It is why friendship can be built on a single well-told story and a plate of food. It is why grief is so exhausting: a library has gone dark, and you keep walking past it, expecting the door to open.

The dog outside has stopped. The man has stopped. They are both looking at something in a hedge—a squirrel, a shadow, a mystery. Then they go on. That might be the whole philosophy: stop when something catches your attention, look long enough to learn its shape, then go on. The trick is not to confuse looking with buying. You do not have to own the mystery. You just have to let it interrupt you.

There is a kind of courage in the ordinary. Getting out of bed when the day is gray. Answering the email. Drinking the water. Saying “I don’t know” instead of inventing. Apologizing in a clear voice. Noticing that the cashier is tired. Leaving a generous tip. These acts do not make good headlines, but they make good Tuesdays, and Tuesdays are where life actually happens. The spectacular is rare by definition; the ordinary is where we practice being human. We practice on cereal boxes and bus schedules, on traffic and small talk, on the slow accumulation of dishes. If the kingdom of heaven is within you, it probably looks like a kitchen after dinner—warm, cluttered, still humming with conversation.

I used to think meaning was a destination. Now I think it is a side effect of attention. The more carefully you look, the more the world seems to look back. Not in a supernatural way, but in the way a face opens when you remember its name. A tree is just a tree until you sit under it for an hour and notice how the leaves hold light like coins in a pocket. A person is just a person until you learn what they are afraid of and why. The world is not short on meaning; it is short on witnesses. We are called to be witnesses—to say, this happened. This mattered. The light fell across the floor like a folded map, and for one second nobody needed to be anywhere else.

So what have I written in these one thousand words? A fence, a window, a dog, a word limit. A small argument for paying attention. Perhaps that is enough. The page will end soon, and the room will continue. The rain will either come or not. The man and the dog will turn some corner. Somewhere a coin will fall into a machine and buy nothing. Somewhere someone will open a door. I hope they leave the light on. I hope we all do. The world is large and strange, and we are brief and bright, and the least we can do is notice one another before the sentence ends.
